guard: every per-agent secret reaches its tenant's segment through ONE migrating choke point, per file and with its whole family; a recorded path may not choose which tenant's material a caller addresses; the deleter that must not migrate still reports both layouts; and `space rm` can reap ONE tenant's secrets - refusing at step 1 where refusing is free, and past step 5 never throwing, never migrating, and never reaching a survivor's material
why: P1's material has a milder failure than P7's - an agent secret read as absent is re-provisioned,
not run beside a live sibling - so the first three mutations grade a slower defect: a canonical
mint beside legacy material nothing will ever reap, on a root that looks healthy the whole time.
Mutation 1 is the read-fallback shipped as an optimization (move only what is already canonical,
which is never); mutation 2 is the refusal swallowed at the P1 placement, which is worse than not
migrating because it converts rule 4's loud stop into a silent skip on exactly the multi-tenant
roots the rule exists for; mutation 3 stops the enumeration skipping DIRECTORIES. That guard is
narrower than it looks and the mutation is aimed at exactly its width: a sibling's `space.<hex>`
segment is already excluded by the SUFFIX filter, so what `isDirectory` alone catches is a
directory NAMED like material (`ghost.creds/`) - and without it `renameSync` is handed a whole
tree to relocate under one tenant's segment. The first cut of this suite asserted the segment
case and this mutant SURVIVED it; the cell that kills it had to be written.
Mutations 4 and 5 hold the two arms of the key prefix apart. The FS arm must resolve through the
choke point rather than compose the string itself - composing it is the read-fallback with extra
steps, and it is what a caller reaching for `agentCredsRoot` writes by accident - while the
hosted arm must answer with the SAME key while moving nothing, because a host provisions from
this string and a flat answer writes where no agent reads.
Mutation 6 is the one that is not about migration at all. `agentSecretKeyForFile` could read the
segment out of the recorded path; it would compile, change no call site, and pass every cell
about paths a caller wrote itself. It would also mean a record written for tenant A can name
tenant B's segment and be handed back a key into it, which the manager then reads, overwrites, or
DELETES. The mutant keeps a check - the segment must still be A segment - so it fails only the
cross-tenant cell, which is the point: the weaker check is the plausible one, and nothing but an
executed cross-tenant probe separates it from the real one.
Mutation 7 grades the deleter. `agentSecretKeysUnder` is root-wide and migration-free by design,
and it must report the pre-P1 FLAT level as well as every tenant's segment. Dropping the flat
level reintroduces this series' own defect inside the sweeper: a `clean all` that leaves an
unmigrated root's agent creds on disk and reports success.
Mutations 8 to 13 grade the `space rm` reap and its precondition (P1 commit 2), which is P7 commit
4's shape at P1's placement - so the mutations aimed at what is DIFFERENT here carry the weight.
Mutation 8 is the reach for the shared PARENT. `auth/creds` holds every tenant's segment, so a
reap addressing it takes every survivor's live agent secrets and reports success; P7's equivalent
mistake (`.cotal/space.*`) needs a glob, this one needs only dropping a `join`.
Mutation 9 is the reaper built on the resolver, and at P1's placement it is WORSE than the
tidiness argument P7 makes. `agentCredsDir` MOVES a pre-P1 flat file into the segment - the very
segment the next line removes - so the reap destroys material that names no tenant, on a
single-tenant root where nothing refuses the move first. That material is exactly what the
precondition exists to protect.
Mutation 10 is the I/O step P7's reap does not have. P7 sweeps a fixed array of four kinds; P1's
key set is OPEN and read off the disk, so there is a `readdirSync` BEFORE the first seam call, and
an unguarded one throws out of a function whose headline contract is that it cannot. Past step 5 a
throw strands the journal entry that gates every other verb and recurs identically on every
re-run, so the removal a crash is supposed to be able to finish could never finish.
Mutation 11 is the reap reusing the root-wide sweep, which is the enumerator already in the file
and the one a reader reaches for. It reports every tenant's keys AND the flat level, so the reap
deletes a survivor's store keys and acts on files that name no owner - a guess, executed.
Mutation 12 points the door at this space's own material instead of the unattributable set. It
compiles, reads plausibly ('check what we are about to reap'), and answers empty on exactly the
root the door exists for.
Mutation 13 is the remedy naming P7's verb. `cotal up` migrates the five P7 kinds and never
touches a P1 resolver, so an operator told to run it and retry finds the files exactly where they
were. This is the `repairAdvice` defect in its P1 form, and only the single-tenant CONTROL cell
separates the honest sentence from the plausible one.

mutations.name: the choke point moves only what is already canonical - the read-fallback, shipped as a cheap gate
mutations.find:
for (const file of legacyAgentSecretFiles(parent)) migrateLegacyMaterialIn(parent, root, space, file);
  return canonical;
mutations.expectRed: all three secret kinds MOVED (canonical present, flat gone)
mutations.cell: first touch moves the legacy family, so no re-provisioning writer ever reads absence past a flat copy

mutations.name: the choke point swallows the shared rules' refusal, per file, and carries on
mutations.expectRed: migration REFUSES on a two-tenant root (rule 4, the same wording as P7's)
mutations.cell: rules 3 and 4 travel OUT through this placement - a caught refusal is a silent skip on the roots the rules exist for

mutations.name: the legacy enumeration stops skipping directories, so a tree named like material is material to move
mutations.expectRed: a DIRECTORY named like material is not material either, so the tree stays where it is
mutations.cell: a directory is never material whatever it is called - the guard the suffix filter does NOT already cover

mutations.name: the FS arm composes the prefix itself instead of going through the choke point
mutations.expectRed: a key builder on the FS arm MOVED the legacy copy on first touch
mutations.cell: every key and path resolves through the one choke point, so first touch reaches every flow rather than the remembered ones

mutations.name: the hosted arm answers with the bare pre-P1 creds dir, as a composition with no root to segment by would
mutations.expectRed: the hosted arm resolves the SAME key shape
mutations.cell: both compositions resolve ONE key - a host provisions from this string, so a flat answer writes where no agent reads

mutations.name: the recorded path's segment is accepted as any segment instead of checked against the caller's space
mutations.expectRed: a path in ANOTHER tenant's segment is refused, and the refusal names that tenant
mutations.cell: the space comes from the caller's authority - a recorded path may not choose which tenant's material is addressed

mutations.name: the sweep reports only the segmented level, stranding an unmigrated root's creds
mutations.expectRed: the pre-P1 FLAT key is reported too (a reset must not strand an unmigrated root)
mutations.cell: the deleter reports BOTH layouts - dropping the flat one is this series' own defect, reintroduced in the sweeper

mutations.name: the reap addresses the SHARED creds parent instead of this tenant's segment
mutations.expectRed: the neighbour tenant's agent secrets are untouched
mutations.cell: one segment, never the parent - `auth/creds` is every tenant's, so reaching for it reaps the survivors

mutations.name: the reap resolves its segment through the choke point, so it migrates what it is about to delete
mutations.expectRed: a pre-P1 flat file is still flat after the reap
mutations.cell: a reaper is a DELETER - resolving would move an unowned file into the segment the next line removes

mutations.name: the reap's enumeration is unguarded, so an unreadable segment throws past the point of no return
mutations.expectRed: an unreadable segment is REPORTED, not thrown past the point of no return
mutations.cell: the OPEN key set puts an I/O step before the first seam call, and it must report rather than throw

mutations.name: the reap enumerates root-wide, taking every tenant's keys and the flat level with them
mutations.expectRed: the per-space enumerator reports only this tenant's segment, never the flat level
mutations.cell: the per-space enumerator is the root-wide sweep MINUS the flat level, and the subtraction is the point

mutations.name: the door weighs this space's own segment instead of the material that names no space
mutations.expectRed: the reap precondition refuses while pre-P1 files sit flat in the creds dir
mutations.cell: the precondition refuses over the UNATTRIBUTABLE set - the one the reap has no right answer for

mutations.name: the remedy names `cotal up`, P7's migration verb, which never touches a P1 resolver
mutations.find: return "Run `cotal doctor auth` for the sole tenant once to move them into its segment, then retry.";
mutations.replace: return "Run `cotal up` for the sole tenant once to migrate it into its own segment, then retry.";
mutations.expectRed: CONTROL: on a single-tenant root the remedy names the verb that actually moves this material
mutations.cell: advice is checked against the verb that actually migrates THIS material, not the neighbouring series'
